cards.explanation: It made large-scale variant identification feasible in clinical genetics.
cards.text: Simultaneously reading many DNA fragments is the basis of {{c1::next-generation sequencing}}.
cards.question: Simultaneously reading many DNA fragments is the basis of {{c1::next-generation sequencing}}.

cards.explanation: The scale of a suspected change influences the choice of test.
cards.text: The branch of genetics concerned with chromosome-level abnormalities is {{c1::cytogenetics}}.
cards.question: The branch of genetics concerned with chromosome-level abnormalities is {{c1::cytogenetics}}.

cards.explanation: Whole-genome sequencing covers a much wider set of regions.
cards.text: Sequencing restricted to the protein-coding exons is called {{c1::exome sequencing}}.
cards.question: Sequencing restricted to the protein-coding exons is called {{c1::exome sequencing}}.

cards.explanation: A reference is a comparison sequence. Differences are expected in healthy people.
cards.text: The lecture estimates that a typical whole genome differs from the reference at roughly {{c1::4–5 million}} positions.
cards.question: The lecture estimates that a typical whole genome differs from the reference at roughly {{c1::4–5 million}} positions.

cards.explanation: Restricting the search to coding regions still leaves many candidates to interpret.
cards.text: The lecture’s exome example yields roughly {{c1::20,000}} differences from the reference.
cards.question: The lecture’s exome example yields roughly {{c1::20,000}} differences from the reference.

cards.explanation: Many differences from the reference sequence are compatible with health.
cards.text: Finding a variant in a patient does not by itself establish its {{c1::pathogenicity}}.
cards.question: Finding a variant in a patient does not by itself establish its {{c1::pathogenicity}}.

cards.explanation: For an inherited disorder, this includes linking a variant to a change in a gene product and then to disease.
cards.text: The study and diagnosis of disease by examining molecules in tissues or body fluids is {{c1::molecular pathology}}.
cards.question: The study and diagnosis of disease by examining molecules in tissues or body fluids is {{c1::molecular pathology}}.

cards.explanation: Effects range from partial reduction to complete absence of activity.
cards.text: A variant that reduces the normal activity of a gene product causes {{c1::loss of function}}.
cards.question: A variant that reduces the normal activity of a gene product causes {{c1::loss of function}}.

cards.explanation: The gain concerns what the product does and need not involve more protein.
cards.text: A variant that creates an abnormal new activity typically produces a {{c1::gain of function}}.
cards.question: A variant that creates an abnormal new activity typically produces a {{c1::gain of function}}.

cards.explanation: Define which function is being measured before assigning a mechanistic label.
cards.text: A permanently open ion channel may have increased ion flow while losing normal {{c1::gating}}.
cards.question: A permanently open ion channel may have increased ion flow while losing normal {{c1::gating}}.

cards.explanation: Inheritance gives a clue to mechanism, with important exceptions.
cards.text: A recessive pedigree can suggest loss of function because one intact allele may supply {{c1::sufficient gene product}}.
cards.question: A recessive pedigree can suggest loss of function because one intact allele may supply {{c1::sufficient gene product}}.

cards.explanation: Different substitutions, truncations or deletions can converge on a similar outcome.
cards.text: Loss-of-function variants often show allelic heterogeneity because many changes can {{c1::disrupt the same function}}.
cards.question: Loss-of-function variants often show allelic heterogeneity because many changes can {{c1::disrupt the same function}}.

cards.explanation: Several distinct changes can disrupt the same essential function.
cards.text: Different variants in the same gene producing the same disorder illustrate {{c1::allelic heterogeneity}}.
cards.question: Different variants in the same gene producing the same disorder illustrate {{c1::allelic heterogeneity}}.

cards.explanation: Haploinsufficiency and dominant-negative effects are two reasons one altered allele can produce disease.
cards.text: Dominant inheritance alone cannot distinguish gain of function from {{c1::dominant loss of function}}.
cards.question: Dominant inheritance alone cannot distinguish gain of function from {{c1::dominant loss of function}}.

cards.explanation: This explains how loss of function can produce a dominant phenotype.
cards.text: Disease caused by one functional copy producing too little product is called {{c1::haploinsufficiency}}.
cards.question: Disease caused by one functional copy producing too little product is called {{c1::haploinsufficiency}}.

cards.explanation: One functional copy may fail to reach the required dosage.
cards.text: Waardenburg syndrome type 1 illustrates how {{c1::haploinsufficiency}} can produce a dominant disorder with many causal alleles.
cards.question: Waardenburg syndrome type 1 illustrates how {{c1::haploinsufficiency}} can produce a dominant disorder with many causal alleles.

cards.explanation: Too little of one component can limit assembly of the entire complex.
cards.text: A protein in a complex with fixed {{c1::stoichiometry}} may be sensitive to reduced gene dosage.
cards.question: A protein in a complex with fixed {{c1::stoichiometry}} may be sensitive to reduced gene dosage.

cards.explanation: The remaining allele can encode a normal protein and still produce too little signal.
cards.text: When a signalling response depends on protein concentration, halving dosage may cross a functional {{c1::threshold}}.
cards.question: When a signalling response depends on protein concentration, halving dosage may cross a functional {{c1::threshold}}.

cards.explanation: The altered product actively disrupts function, for example within a protein complex.
cards.text: A mutant protein that interferes with its normal counterpart has a {{c1::dominant-negative}} effect.
cards.question: A mutant protein that interferes with its normal counterpart has a {{c1::dominant-negative}} effect.

cards.explanation: The mutant subunit may compromise complexes containing normal subunits.
cards.text: A null allele makes no functional product. A dominant-negative allele can be more disruptive because it {{c1::interferes with normal protein}}.
cards.question: A null allele makes no functional product. A dominant-negative allele can be more disruptive because it {{c1::interferes with normal protein}}.

cards.explanation: This can have a greater effect than simply making fewer normal chains.
cards.text: In severe osteogenesis imperfecta, an abnormal collagen chain can disrupt {{c1::assembly of the collagen molecule}}.
cards.question: In severe osteogenesis imperfecta, an abnormal collagen chain can disrupt {{c1::assembly of the collagen molecule}}.

cards.explanation: This illustrates a dosage defect and explains the contrast with a structural collagen defect.
cards.text: In the lecture’s type I osteogenesis imperfecta example, the primary problem is reduced {{c1::quantity of normal collagen}}.
cards.question: In the lecture’s type I osteogenesis imperfecta example, the primary problem is reduced {{c1::quantity of normal collagen}}.

cards.explanation: Recurrence of a variant alone cannot establish what it does to the protein.
cards.text: Finding the same causal variant in many affected people is called allelic {{c1::homogeneity}}.
cards.question: Finding the same causal variant in many affected people is called allelic {{c1::homogeneity}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: Timing can change the biological effect even when the protein sequence is intact.
cards.text: Gene expression at the wrong developmental time is described as {{c1::heterochronic}} expression.
cards.question: Gene expression at the wrong developmental time is described as {{c1::heterochronic}} expression.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: The location of activity can be as important as its level.
cards.text: Gene expression in a tissue where it is normally absent is called {{c1::ectopic}} expression.
cards.question: Gene expression in a tissue where it is normally absent is called {{c1::ectopic}} expression.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: Consider the stimulus as well as the magnitude of the response.
cards.text: A protein responding to an inappropriate {{c1::signal}} can acquire abnormal activity without gaining a new catalytic function.
cards.question: A protein responding to an inappropriate {{c1::signal}} can acquire abnormal activity without gaining a new catalytic function.

cards.explanation: This is one mechanism through which a receptor variant can confer gain of function.
cards.text: A receptor that signals without its ligand is {{c1::constitutively active}}.
cards.question: A receptor that signals without its ligand is {{c1::constitutively active}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: Inappropriate signalling can mimic a hormone response before the usual developmental stage.
cards.text: Familial male precocious puberty illustrates gain of function in a hormone {{c1::receptor}}.
cards.question: Familial male precocious puberty illustrates gain of function in a hormone {{c1::receptor}}.

cards.explanation: Different alleles of the same gene can cause loss or gain of function.
cards.text: The functional effect must be assigned to the specific {{c1::variant}} even when the disease gene is known.
cards.question: The functional effect must be assigned to the specific {{c1::variant}} even when the disease gene is known.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: Other proteins, tissues and feedback systems influence how a molecular change presents.
cards.text: To progress from protein dysfunction to a clinical phenotype, trace the affected {{c1::biological pathways}}.
cards.question: To progress from protein dysfunction to a clinical phenotype, trace the affected {{c1::biological pathways}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: Loss of function spans a continuum from partial to complete.
cards.text: Two loss-of-function alleles can differ in severity if they retain different amounts of {{c1::residual activity}}.
cards.question: Two loss-of-function alleles can differ in severity if they retain different amounts of {{c1::residual activity}}.

cards.explanation: Their effects can depend on gene dosage and on which sequences the breakpoints disrupt.
cards.text: Large deletions, duplications and inversions are examples of {{c1::structural variation}}.
cards.question: Large deletions, duplications and inversions are examples of {{c1::structural variation}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: A copy-number count alone does not establish that a rearrangement is harmless.
cards.text: An inversion can leave gene dosage unchanged while disrupting a gene at a {{c1::breakpoint}}.
cards.question: An inversion can leave gene dosage unchanged while disrupting a gene at a {{c1::breakpoint}}.

cards.explanation: Absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion can all affect exposure.
cards.text: Genetic effects on what the body does to a drug concern {{c1::pharmacokinetics}}.
cards.question: Genetic effects on what the body does to a drug concern {{c1::pharmacokinetics}}.

cards.explanation: Two patients with similar drug exposure can still have different responses.
cards.text: Genetic effects on how a target responds to a drug concern {{c1::pharmacodynamics}}.
cards.question: Genetic effects on how a target responds to a drug concern {{c1::pharmacodynamics}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: For the same dose, slower clearance can increase drug exposure.
cards.text: If a variant slows the metabolism of a medicine, the affected process is {{c1::pharmacokinetics}}.
cards.question: If a variant slows the metabolism of a medicine, the affected process is {{c1::pharmacokinetics}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: The distinction concerns the effect at a given exposure.
cards.text: If two people have the same drug concentration but different receptor responses, the difference is {{c1::pharmacodynamic}}.
cards.question: If two people have the same drug concentration but different receptor responses, the difference is {{c1::pharmacodynamic}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: It can inform both drug choice and dosing.
cards.text: The discipline examining how genetic variation affects drug action is {{c1::pharmacogenomics}}.
cards.question: The discipline examining how genetic variation affects drug action is {{c1::pharmacogenomics}}.

cards.explanation: The molecular cause of a disorder can guide treatment selection.
cards.text: Tailoring care to individual biological and clinical differences is called {{c1::precision medicine}}.
cards.question: Tailoring care to individual biological and clinical differences is called {{c1::precision medicine}}.

cards.topic: Gain of function and clinical effects
cards.explanation: A treatment that corrects one mechanism may have little effect on another.
cards.text: A molecular diagnosis can guide treatment selection when patients sharing a clinical diagnosis have different {{c1::disease mechanisms}}.
cards.question: A molecular diagnosis can guide treatment selection when patients sharing a clinical diagnosis have different {{c1::disease mechanisms}}.
